⟦picture 1⟧

[The Prima Porta statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_of_Prima_Porta) of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus) (<u>r.</u> 27 BC – AD 14), the first [Roman emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor)

The [Roman emperors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor) were the rulers of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire) from the granting of the name and title [*Augustus*](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_(title)>) to [Octavian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus) by the [Roman Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate) in 27 BC onward. Augustus maintained a facade of Republican rule, rejecting monarchical titles calling himself [*princeps senatus*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeps_senatus) (first man of the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Roman_Empire)) and *princeps civitatis* (first citizen of the state). The title of Augustus was conferred on his successors to the imperial position, and emperors gradually grew more monarchical and authoritarian.

The style of government instituted by Augustus is called the [Principate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principate) and continued until the late third or early fourth century. The modern word "emperor" derives from the title [*imperator*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperator), that was granted by an army to a successful general; during the initial phase of the empire, the title was generally used only by the [*princeps*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeps). For example, Augustus officially styled himself as *Imperator Caesar* [*Divi Filius*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divi_Filius) *Augustus*. The territory under command of the emperor had developed under the period of the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic) as it invaded and occupied much of [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe) and portions of [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa) and the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East). Under the republic, the [Senate and People of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPQR) authorized provincial governors, who answered only to them, to rule regions of the empire. The chief magistrates of the republic were two [consuls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul) elected each year; consuls continued to be elected in the imperial period, but their authority was subservient to that of the emperor, who also controlled and determined their election. Often, the emperors themselves, or close family, were selected as consul.

After the [Crisis of the Third Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century), [Diocletian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian) increased the authority of the emperor and adopted the title [*dominus noster*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominus_noster) (our lord). The rise of powerful [barbarian tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbarian#In_classical_Greco-Roman_contexts) along the borders of the empire, the challenge they posed to the defense of far-flung borders as well as an unstable imperial succession led Diocletian to divide the administration of the Empire geographically with a co-*augustus* in 286. In 330, [Constantine the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_the_Great), the emperor who accepted Christianity, established a second capital in [Byzantium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantium), which was renamed [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople). Historians consider the [Dominate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominate) period of the empire to have begun with either Diocletian or Constantine, depending on the author. For most of the period from 286 to 480, there was more than one recognized senior emperor, with the division usually based on geographic regions. This division became permanent after the death of [Theodosius I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I) in 395, which historians have traditionally dated as the division between the [Western Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire) and the [Eastern Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire). However, formally the Empire remained a single polity, with separate co-emperors in the separate courts.

The [fall of the Western Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire) is dated either from the [*de facto*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto) date of 476, when [Romulus Augustulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus) was deposed by the [Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_peoples) [Herulians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heruli) led by [Odoacer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer), or the [*de jure*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_jure) date of 480, on the death of [Julius Nepos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Nepos), when Eastern emperor [Zeno](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeno_(emperor)>) ended recognition of a separate Western court. Historians typically refer to the empire in the centuries that followed as the "[Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire)", governed by the Byzantine emperors. Given that "Byzantine" is a later [historiographical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography) designation and the inhabitants and emperors of the empire continually maintained [Roman identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_identity), this designation is not used universally and continues to be a subject of specialist debate. Under [Justinian I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I), in the sixth century, a large portion of the western empire was retaken, including Italy, Africa, and part of Spain. Over the course of the centuries thereafter, most of the imperial territories were lost, which eventually restricted the empire to [Anatolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatolia) and the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans). The line of emperors continued until the death of [Constantine XI Palaiologos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_XI_Palaiologos) at the [fall of Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople) in 1453, when the remaining territories were conquered by the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire) led by Sultan [Mehmed II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmed_II). In the aftermath of the conquest, Mehmed II proclaimed himself *kayser-i Rûm* ("[*Caesar*](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar_(title)>) of the Romans"), thus claiming to be the new emperor, [a claim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_claim_to_Roman_succession) maintained by succeeding sultans. Competing claims of [succession to the Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_of_the_Roman_Empire) have also been forwarded by various other states and empires, and by numerous [later pretenders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_to_the_Byzantine_Empire#Claims_to_descent_and_inheritance).

## Legitimacy

*See also:* [*Roman emperor*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor) *and* [*Roman usurper*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_usurper)

⟦picture 2⟧

Coin of [Pescennius Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pescennius_Niger), a [Roman usurper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_usurper) who claimed imperial power AD 193–194. Legend: IMP CAES C PESC NIGER IVST AVG

While the imperial government of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire) was rarely called into question during its five centuries in the west and fifteen centuries in the east, individual emperors often faced unending challenges in the form of usurpation and perpetual civil wars. From the rise of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus), the first Roman emperor, in 27 BC to the [sack of Rome](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(455)>) in AD 455, there were over a hundred usurpations or attempted usurpations (an average of one usurpation or attempt about every four years). From the murder of [Commodus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodus) in 192 until the fifth century, there was scarcely a single decade without succession conflicts and civil war. Very few emperors died of natural causes, with [regicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regicide) in practical terms having become the expected end of a Roman emperor by [late antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_antiquity). The distinction between a usurper and a legitimate emperor is a blurry one, given that a large number of emperors that were commonly considered legitimate began their rule as usurpers, revolting against the previous legitimate emperor.

True legitimizing structures and theories were weak, or wholly absent in the Roman Empire, and there were no true objective legal criteria for being acclaimed emperor beyond acceptance by the [Roman army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_army). Dynastic succession was not legally formalized, but also not uncommon, with powerful rulers sometimes succeeding in passing power on to their children or other relatives. While dynastic ties could bring someone to the throne, they were not a guarantee that their rule would not be challenged. Control of [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome) itself and approval of the [Roman Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate) held some importance as legitimising factors, but were mostly symbolic. Emperors who began their careers as usurpers had often been deemed [public enemies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_enemy) by the senate before they managed to take the city. Emperors did not need to be acclaimed or crowned in Rome itself, as demonstrated in the [Year of the Four Emperors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Four_Emperors) (69), when claimants were crowned by armies in the [Roman provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_province), and the senate's role in legitimising emperors had almost faded into insignificance by the [Crisis of the Third Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century) (235–285). By the end of the third century, Rome's importance was mainly ideological, with several emperors and usurpers even beginning to place their court in other cities in the empire, closer to the imperial frontier.

Common methods used by emperors to assert claims of legitimacy, such as proclamation by the army, blood connections (sometimes fictitious) to past emperors, wearing imperial regalia, distributing one's own coins or statues and claims to pre-eminent virtue through propaganda, were pursued just as well by many usurpers as they were by legitimate emperors. There were no constitutional or legal distinctions that differentiated legitimate emperors and usurpers. In ancient Roman texts, the differences between emperors and "tyrants" (the term typically used for usurpers) is often a moral one (with the tyrants ascribed wicked behaviour) rather than a legal one. Typically, the actual distinction was whether the claimant had been victorious or not. In the [*Historia Augusta*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_Augusta), an ancient Roman collection of imperial biographies, the usurper [Pescennius Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pescennius_Niger) (193–194) is expressly noted to only be a tyrant because he was defeated by [Septimius Severus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septimius_Severus) (<u>r.</u> 193–211). This is also followed in modern [historiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography), where, in the absence of constitutional criteria separating them, the main factor that distinguishes usurpers from legitimate Roman emperors is their degree of success. What makes a figure who began as a usurper into a legitimate emperor is typically either that they managed to gain the recognition from a more senior, legitimate emperor, or that they managed to defeat a more senior, legitimate emperor and seize power from them by force.

### List inclusion criteria

Given that a concept of constitutional legitimacy was irrelevant in the Roman Empire, and emperors were only 'legitimate' in so far as they were able to be accepted in the wider empire, this list of emperors operates on a collection of inclusion criteria:

- Imperial claimants whose power across the empire became, or from the beginning was, absolute and who ruled undisputed are treated as legitimate emperors. From 286 onward, when imperial power was usually divided among two colleagues in the east and west, control over the respective half is sufficient even if a claimant was not recognized in the other half, such as was the case for several of the last few emperors in the west.
- Imperial claimants who were proclaimed emperors by another, legitimate, senior emperor, or who were recognized by a legitimate senior emperor, are treated as legitimate emperors. Many emperors ruled alongside one or various joint-emperors. However, and specially from the 4th century onwards, most of these were children who never ruled in their own right. Scholars of the later Empire always omit these rulers, but the same is not always applied during the early Empire. For the purposes of consistency, later senior emperors' tenures as junior co-emperors are not counted as part of their reign. The list also gives all co-emperors their own entry only up to the 4th century.
- Imperial claimants who achieved the recognition of the Roman Senate, especially in times of uncertainty and civil war, are, due to the senate's nominal role as an elective body, treated as legitimate emperors. In later times, especially when emperors ruled from other cities, this criterion defaults to the possession and control of Rome itself. In the later eastern empire, possession of the capital of [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople) was an essential element of imperial legitimacy.

In the case of non-dynastic emperors after or in the middle of the rule of a dynasty, it is customary among historians to group them together with the rulers of said dynasty, an approach that is followed in this list. Dynastic breaks with non-dynastic rulers are indicated with thickened horizontal lines.

### Laskaris dynasty, in Nicaea (1205–1261)

*Main articles:* [*Laskaris*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laskaris) *and* [*Empire of Nicaea*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Nicaea)

***Note:*** *Roman rule in Constantinople was interrupted with the* [*capture and sack of the city*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople) *by the* [*crusaders*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade) *in 1204, which led to the establishment of the* [*Frankokratia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankokratia)*. Though the crusaders created a new line of* [*Latin emperors*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_emperor) *in the city, modern historians recognize the line of emperors of the Laskaris dynasty, reigning in* [*Nicaea*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Nicaea)*, as the legitimate Roman emperors during the* [*struggle for Constantinople*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_for_Constantinople) *because the Nicene Empire eventually retook the city. For other lines of claimant emperors, see* [*List of Trapezuntine emperors*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Trapezuntine_emperors) *and* [*List of Thessalonian emperors*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Thessalonian_emperors)*.*

## Other claims to the Roman imperial title

*See also:* [*Succession of the Roman Empire*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_of_the_Roman_Empire) *and* [*Succession to the Byzantine Empire*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_to_the_Byzantine_Empire)

**Other claims to the Roman imperial title**

| Subject | Description |
| :-: | :-: |
| Roman usurpers ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_usurpers)) | [Roman usurpers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_usurper) were individuals or groups of individuals who obtained or tried to obtain power by force and without [legitimate](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legitimacy_(political)>) legal authority. [Usurpation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usurpation) was endemic during the [Roman imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire) era, especially from the [crisis of the third century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_third_century) onwards, when political instability became the rule.<br>A number of individuals proclaimed themselves emperor (or were proclaimed or appointed as emperor), but are not considered as legitimate emperors because they did not oust the ruling emperor, or did not establish control of the whole empire, or were not accepted by the senate or other imperial colleagues. |
| Byzantine usurpers ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Byzantine_usurpers)) |  |
| Holy Roman Emperors ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor#List_of_emperors)) | The [Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor) was the ruler and [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state) of the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire).<br>[Charlemagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne) was crowned *imperator romanorum* ("Emperor of the Romans") by [Pope Leo III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_III) in AD 800. In so doing, the Pope rejected the legitimacy of [Empress Irene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Irene). The Byzantines never recognized the Holy Roman emperors as "Roman" and called them the "emperor ([*basileus*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basileus)) of the Franks"; to them only the [Byzantine Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Senate) (successor to the [Roman Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate)) and/or the [Byzantine military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_military) (successor to the [Roman military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_military)) had the right to appoint a new Roman emperor. Likewise, Western Europeans didn't recognize the legitimacy of the Byzantine emperors and called them the 'emperor of the Greeks' or the 'emperor of Constantinople'. See also: [Problem of two emperors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problem_of_two_emperors) |
| Latin Emperors ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Emperor)) | The [Latin Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Emperor) was the ruler of the [Latin Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Empire), the historiographical convention for the [Crusader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades) realm, established in [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople) after the [Fourth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade) (1204) and lasting until the city was recovered by the [Byzantine Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Greeks) in 1261. Its name derives from its [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic) and Western European ("[Latin](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latins_(Middle_Ages)>)") nature. The empire, whose official name was *Imperium Romaniae* ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin): "Empire of [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire)"), claimed the direct heritage of the [Eastern Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire), which had most of its lands taken and partitioned by the crusaders. This claim however was disputed by the Byzantine Greek successor states, the [Empire of Nicaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Nicaea), the [Empire of Trebizond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Trebizond) and the [Despotate of Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Epirus). Out of these three, the Nicaeans succeeded in displacing the Latin emperors in 1261 and restored the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire). |
| Trapezuntine emperors ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Trapezuntine_emperors)) | The [Trapezuntine emperors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trapezuntine_emperors) were the rulers of the [Empire of Trebizond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Trebizond), one of the successor states of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire) founded after the [Fourth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade) in 1204, until [its fall](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Trebizond_(1461)>) to the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire) in 1461. The rulers of Trebizond called themselves [*Megas Komnenos*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Komnenos) and – like their counterparts in the other two Byzantine successor states, the [Empire of Nicaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Nicaea) and the [Despotate of Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Epirus) – initially claimed supremacy as "Emperor and Autocrat of the Romans". However, after [Michael VIII Palaiologos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_VIII_Palaiologos) of Nicaea recaptured Constantinople in 1261, the Komnenian use of the style "Emperor" became a sore point. In September 1282, at Constantinople, [John II of Trebizond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Trebizond) relinquished his claim and accepted the title [despot](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despot_(court_title)>). His successors used a variant of the imperial title, "Emperor and Autocrat of all the East, [the Iberians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasian_Iberia), and the [Transmarine Provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perateia)" until the Empire's end in 1461. |
| Trapezuntine usurpers ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Trapezuntine_usurpers)) | Trapzeuntine usurpers were individuals or groups of individuals who obtained or tried to obtain power by force and without [legitimate](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legitimacy_(political)>) legal authority. [Usurpation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usurpation) became an endemic during the [Trapezuntine Civil Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trapezuntine_Civil_Wars?action=edit&redlink=1) and other cases of political instability in the [Empire of Trebizond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Trebizond). |
| Emperors of Thessalonica ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Thessalonica#Rulers)) | The emperors of Thessalonica were the rulers of the [Empire of Thessalonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Thessalonica), a [historiographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiographic) term to refer to the short-lived state centred on the city of [Thessalonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessalonica) between 1224 and 1246 ([*sensu stricto*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensu_stricto) until 1242) and ruled by the [Komnenodoukas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komnenodoukas) of [Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Epirus). |
| Despots of Epirus ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despot_of_Epirus#List_of_despots_of_Epirus,_1205%E2%80%931479)) | The [despot of Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despot_of_Epirus) was the ruler of the [Despotate of Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Epirus), one of the successor states of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire) in the aftermath of the [Fourth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade). The name "Despotate of Epirus" is a modern historiographical name and was not used at the time.<br>Some rulers used the version "[despot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotes) of Romania" (Romania essentially referring to the territories of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire), i.e. Byzantium) or "despot of the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhomaioi)" (claiming rulership over the Romans, i.e. the Byzantines/Greeks). |
| Despot of Epirus usurpers ([list](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Epirote_usurpers_(Despotate_of_Epirus)>)) | Despot of Epirus usurpers were individuals or groups of individuals who obtained or tried to obtain power by force and without [legitimate](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legitimacy_(political)>) legal authority in the Despotate of Epirus. |
| Ottoman sultans ([list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sultans_of_the_Ottoman_Empire)) | After the [conquest of Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Constantinople) in 1453, the Ottoman sultans adopted the title of Roman Emperors, or more preciselly *Kayser-i Rum*, literally "[Caesar](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar_(title)>) of the Romans", the standard title for earlier Byzantine Emperors in Arab, Persian and Turkish languages.. Based on the concept of [right of conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_conquest), the sultans of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire) claimed to be the legitimate Roman Emperors, in succession to the Byzantine emperors who had previously ruled from Constantinople. This claim was recognized by other powers of the [Islamic world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world), for example the [Safavid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Empire) (Persia) and the [Mughal Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire) (India), and by the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty) and [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty) of China, but was never recognized by the Western Europeans. See [Ottoman claim to Roman succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_claim_to_Roman_succession) |

## Notes

1. The term [*basileus*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basileus) eventually replaced [*augustus*](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_(title)>) as the official title of the emperor, although both were seen as equals already by the times of [Constantine I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_I).
2. The Byzantine Empire is universally recognized as the remnant, continuation or later stage of the Roman Empire. There is no universally agreed date used to separate the ancient Roman and "Byzantine" empires, with proposed dates ranging in age from 284 to 717. Some authors reject the term "Byzantine" entirely.
3. Spain was lost in 625 and Africa in 698. A large portion of Italy was conquered by the [Lombards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombards) already under Justinian I's successor, [Justin II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_II). Rome and its surroundings remained under imperial control until 756, when they became the [Papal States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_States), though the last Italian holdouts were not lost until 1071 with the [fall of Bari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Bari). The seventh century also saw much of the empire's eastern and southern territories lost permanently to [Arab Muslim conquests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spread_of_Islam).
4. There is no generally-accepted count of Roman emperors given that different scholars sometimes include and omit different emperors (see [Legitimacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_emperors#Legitimacy)). This list includes 174 emperors, 11 of whose legitimacy is disputed in scholarship (also including the four [emperors of Nicaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Nicaea), who are often seen as the "legitimate" emperors during the interregnum of 1204–1261), and 4 ruling empresses for a total of 178 monarchs. Also included are 34 junior co-emperors, 1 [emperor-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Kanabos), 1 [junior co-empress](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thekla_(daughter_of_Theophilos)>), and 2 co-empresses in [Thessalonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessalonica). All in all, this list thus includes a total of 216 occupants of the Roman imperial office.
5. This was one of the titles used for the emperors in Constantinople by Ottoman writers prior to 1453.
6. Entries also include the [regnal name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regnal_name) of each emperor. These generally differed from their birth name, often adopting elements from the previous emperor. [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus)'s full name would be "Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus" according to [Roman naming conventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_naming_conventions) ("Octavian" was a nickname), but he styled himself as "[Imperator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperator) Caesar Augustus", treating "Caesar" as a family name. Given that "Imperator" was only a victory title, it will be omitted from the emperors' full nomenclature.
7. The conventional date for the Empire's founding is 27 BC, when the Senate awarded Octavian the title and name [*Augustus*](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_(title)>) alongside one of several grants of power. Ancient writers, however, give him a rule of 56 years. He became [*de facto*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto) monarch in 31 BC, after defeating his last remaining opposition at the [Battle of Actium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Actium). This is a date also used by some writers. Augustus himself dated his accession to legal power to 7 January 43 BC, when he first received [*imperium*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperium). Later that year he became [consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul) (19 August) and then [triumvir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Triumvirate) (27 November) alongside [Mark Antony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Antony) and [Lepidus](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aemilius_Lepidus_(triumvir)>). Augustus thus ruled the Roman state for exactly 56 years, but only 40 as "emperor".
8. By this time, '[Caesar](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar_(title)>)' and '[Augustus](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_(title)>)' are regarded less as personal names and more as imperial titles, with the former denoting the heir-apparent and the latter indicating the emperor himself.
9. The date of his acclamation is usually given as 27 November 176. This is the day in which he was proclaimed *imperator* and Commodus himself appears to have considered it the beginning of his reign. Some scholars argue that his actual reign as *augustus* began later, as he does not appear in official documents of early 177.
10. The junior co-emperors marked as being of "varying ascribed status" are figures, mostly children, who are usually not counted as "true" emperors given their submissive status to the senior emperor, but are still present in some lists of rulers.
11. Unless otherwise noted to be some other ambiguity, the emperors marked to be of ambiguous legitimacy are those who fulfill one or more of the inclusion criteria above, but who are not universally regarded by scholars to count as legitimate. In most cases, such figures are those who held power only briefly, and/or who in times of more than one emperor held one of the capitals but never achieved the full recognition of the other emperor(s).
12. On account of the limited surviving source material, almost all dates used here are just approximate. The chronology of the whole period is dubious and sources rarely agree on each other, in part due to the fact that many reigns overlap due to most emperors starting as rivals. For an analysis of the chronology, see [Rea 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_emperors#CITEREFRea1972), [Peachin 1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_emperors#CITEREFPeachin1990) and [Burgess 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_emperors#CITEREFBurgess2014).
13. Unattested in coinage; only briefly mentioned by [Aurelius Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelius_Victor) and [Cyprian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprian) (the latter indirectly).
14. Unmentioned in literary sources and known only from two coins seemingly issued in Rome, implying he was proclaimed emperor in the capital, probably between Aemilianus and Valerian, or against either.
15. Made *caesar* by his father and only referred to as *augustus* in a single series of coins, issued while he was besieged in [Cologne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne) in 260. Coinage issued after his death lack any title; probably because Gallienus did not want to advertise the death of a second emperor in one year. It is unclear whether his acclamation was ever recognized (or even known) by Gallienus, but if he had survived it would surely have been recognized (like [Valentinian II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentinian_II), who was proclaimed by the army but was accepted by [Gratian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratian)).
16. The chronology of Maximian's career is disputed. Some authors argue that he was promoted to *augustus* without ever being *caesar*, as claimed by many others. Another possible date for his accession as emperor (and the first division of the Roman Empire) is 13 December 285.
17. The extent to which Constantine supported [Domitius Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domitius_Alexander) is disputed. It appears that Constantine never officially recognized him as emperor, but still offered some cautious support as a way to pressure Maxentius.
18. Legitimately appointed as co-emperor by Licinius, though as western emperor (in opposition to Constantine I). Referred as *caesar* in literary sources, but called *augustus* in coinage. Did not actually rule anything given that Licinius did not control the west.
19. Although technically recognized by Constantius II, who even sent him the imperial [diadem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diadem), Vetranio is often regarded as a usurper.
20. From the fourth century, emperors and other high-profile men of non-aristocratic birth often bore the name "Flavius", the family name of the Constantinian dynasty. Because it was often used as a status marker rather than personal name, "Flavius" will generally be omitted in the following entries for simplicity.
21. Distinction between [*nomen*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen_gentilicium), [*praenomen*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praenomen) and [*cognomen*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognomen), the core elements of [Roman naming conventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_naming_conventions), began to fade away from the 3rd century onwards. Given that "new Romans" —that is, [barbarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbarian#In_classical_Greco-Roman_contexts) turned [citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_citizenship)— adopted the names of their masters, many citizens adopted the names [Julius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_gens), [Flavius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavian_dynasty) (notable the [Constantinians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinian_dynasty)) and [Marcus Aurelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nerva%E2%80%93Antonine_dynasty) (notable the 3rd century emperors), thus making them obsolete as [surnames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surnames). As a result, most citizens of the Empire, even emperors, reverted back to single-names by the 5th century.
22. Although they constitutionally held the same supreme power as their senior counterpart, it is customary among scholars of the later empire to only regard those who actually ruled as emperors, omitting junior co-emperors who only exercised power nominally and never governed in their own name. Most of these co-emperors were children that barely appear in historical records.
23. There is particular confusion surrounding the name "Constantine III", as it has been applied to both a Western ([Constantine](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_III_(Western_Roman_emperor)>)) and an Eastern emperor ([Heraclius Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraclius_Constantine)). Heraclius Constantine is often enumerated as 'Constantine III', but this name is also often applied to the earlier western emperor and has also been used for Heraclius Constantine's son [Constans II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constans_II) (who actually ruled under the name 'Constantine', 'Constans' being a nickname).
24. From 629 onwards, Heraclius issued administrative documents in Greek. Latin continued to be used in communication with Western Europe until the end of the empire and coins continued to be struck with Latin inscriptions until the early eighth century.
25. Tiberius and Heraclius were crowned by their father [Constans II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constans_II) on 2 June 659, likely as babies. Constantine tried to get rid of his brothers as soon as they came of age, but the army rioted. He initially accepted, but quickly turn against the leaders of the revolt and executed them. Then, around October 681, [cut Tiberius and Heraclius’ noses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_mutilation_in_Byzantine_culture), a common Byzantine punishment that disqualified anyone from the throne.
26. Latin ceased being used in coin inscriptions under Leo III.
27. Most of miniature portraits used for the 9th to 11th centuries are not contemporary, but taken from the 12th-century [*Madrid Skylitzes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Skylitzes). The portrait of [Nikephoros I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikephoros_I) is taken from the [*Manasses Chronicle*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manasses_Chronicle) (<u>c.</u> 1345), while the portrait of [Nikephoros II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikephoros_II) is taken from a 15th-century miniature of uncertain origin. All of these portraits are almost certainly imaginary. The 15th-century [*Mutinensis gr. 122*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutinensis_gr._122) is used for some 11th-century emperors with no surviving portrait, although these are probably imaginary as well.
28. Theodora's daughter Thekla appears to have been formally associated with Theodora and Michael III in the government of the Empire, although almost nothing is known about her actual role during her mother's rule.
29. Son of Christopher and grandson of Romanos I; unattested in official documents and only briefly mentioned by [Michael Psellos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Psellos) and [Joannes Zonaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joannes_Zonaras). He was probably crowned as a baby but died shortly after, certainly before 927.
30. Most emperors began to officially use family names from Constantine IX Monomachos onwards. Michael VI notably avoided using his surname, Bringas, because it was far less distinguished than those of the other imperial families.
31. Some historians regard Eudokia as an empress regnant, while others consider her as a regent.
32. Unattested in official documents; Leo is only called emperor in a singular letter, while his brother's status can only be deduced from the fact that he was [born in the purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_in_the_purple) and that he also used the "imperial tokens".
33. Constantine Doukas notably served as junior co-emperor of two emperors, first his father Michael VII and then Alexios I, who briefly restored his rights. As always, this was only symbolical, as Constantine remained a minor during both tenures, having been crowned as a newborn. He died on 12 August 1094, aged around 20 years old.
34. The identification of this figure from Vat. Gr. 1851 as Alexios II is by Ioannis Spatharakis. Other historians variously identify him as a young [Andronikos IV Palaiologos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andronikos_IV_Palaiologos) or [Andronikos II Palaiologos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andronikos_II_Palaiologos).
35. Many of the miniature portraits used for the late Byzantine period are not contemporary, but taken from the [*Codex Mutinensis graecus 122*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutinensis_gr._122), completed <u>c.</u> 1425 and expanded after 1453. The codex depicts almost every single Roman emperor from [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus) to [Constantine XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_XI), but only the later portraits are considered reliable, especially those of the [Palaiologoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaiologoi). The accuracy of earlier portraits is disputed, but at least from [Heraclius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraclius) onwards they appear to be based on sources available to their author.
36. Alexios III used the name Alexios Komnenos Angelos (Ἀλέξιος Κομνηνός Ἄγγελος) prior to his accession but reigned as Alexios Komnenos, dropping his own family name in order to stress his matrilineal descent from the Komnenos dynasty.
37. Unattested in coins, Nicholas is called "emperor and heir" in a single document. He died soon after, less than 10 years old.
38. It has been argued that [Constantine Laskaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_Laskaris), Theodore's brother, ruled for a time after April 1204. According to [Nicetas Choniates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicetas_Choniates), Constantine was proclaimed emperor by the remaining [Varangian Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varangian_Guard) at [Hagia Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia). However, he also notes that Constantine ultimately refused the imperial insignia, and the populace and army quickly ignored him. Constantine is not attested as emperor of Nicaea in any known source. The date of Theodore's proclamation as emperor is also uncertain. Modern authors often date it to 1205. However, contemporary sources imply a late date in 1204. One manuscript credits Theodore with a rule of 17 years and 3 months, while the historian [George Akropolites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Akropolites) gives him 18 years.
39. During the last years of the Empire, the territory of [Thessalonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessalonica) was effectively ruled as separate realm from Constantinople. Two empresses, [Irene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_of_Montferrat) and [Anna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_of_Savoy), took residence there, even having their own courts and ruling as *de facto* empresses regnant. Anna notably ruled in Thessalonica in opposition to [John VI Kantakouzenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_VI_Kantakouzenos), who later recognized her portion of the empire.
40. [Michael IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_IX) is often listed as full emperor (rather than co-emperor) in modern sources, although he never reigned in his own name. He appears to have used the title of [*autokrator*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autokrator) alongside his father, which implied an equal status.
41. [Matthew Kantakouzenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Kantakouzenos), already an adult, was given part of [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace) by his father [John VI Kantakouzenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_VI_Kantakouzenos) as an appanage in 1343. He was crowned co-emperor in April 1353, during his father's war against [John V Palaiologos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V_Palaiologos). Matthew retained his Thracian domains until December 1357, when he abdicated following a military defeat against the [Serbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbs). John V later appointed him as [despot of the Morea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despot_of_the_Morea).
42. John VII inherited his father's lands around Selymbria and, as per a 1381 agreement with Andronikos IV that legitimized his role as co-emperor and heir. He ruled there with the title of emperor (*basileus*), although he ruled heavily influenced by the Ottomans and [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Genoa).
43. Manuel, who previously had been given governorship over Thessalonica and had already been crowned co-emperor, set up an independent court and ruled there as *basileus* instead of [*despotes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotes). Manuel ruled in opposition of his father's soft policies towards the Ottomans, waging war upon them. However, the city eventually fell and Manuel had to flee in shame.
44. This depiction of John VIII is from the [Magi Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magi_Chapel), which was painted in 1459–1461 (about a decade after his death) by [Benozzo Gozzoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benozzo_Gozzoli). Gozzoli likely saw John in person at the [Council of Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Florence). He also seems to have used [a contemporary medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_John_VIII_Palaeologus) by [Pisanello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisanello) as a source.
